question: How can a park help clean stormwater before it reaches a river?
hook: A park can be part of a city’s water system.
company_copy: O2 is a planning and design practice with a Calgary studio. At Dale Hodges Park, it worked with other specialists to combine stormwater treatment, habitat and public space. Its project account describes marshes, wet meadows and landforms that guide water before it reaches the Bow River. This was collaborative work; O2 did not design every element alone.
local_note: Calgary studio; the featured project is Dale Hodges Park in Calgary.
classroom_steps: Runoff carries water and suspended material from streets into drainage systems.
At Dale Hodges Park, water follows a designed route through a landscape rather than remaining hidden in pipes.
Slower flow can allow some suspended particles to settle. Different treatment stages address different parts of the problem.
The landscape also supports habitat and recreation. A useful design must account for these needs together.
discussion: Would the clearest-looking water necessarily be the safest water?
activity: Draw two fictional routes from a street drain to a river: one short and fast, one with space for settling. Mark where to sample and one habitat trade-off.
teacher_note: Clear water can still contain dissolved contaminants. This is a planning model, not a drinking-water treatment demonstration.

question: How can you support a library above a moving train?
hook: The space below a building can be just as important as the rooms inside it.
company_copy: Entuitive provided structural engineering for Calgary’s Central Library. Its Calgary-based project lead describes the challenge of building above an active LRT corridor using long-span trusses and coordinating construction with transit operations. Structural engineering helps the building carry loads while leaving space for the railway. The architect, builder and transit operator had different responsibilities.
local_note: Calgary project and a Calgary-based structural engineering lead are explicitly documented.
classroom_steps: A building’s weight and the people inside create loads that must reach the ground.
An active rail corridor limits where supports can go. The structure has to span the space.
Truss members and connections transfer forces along a designed load path. Construction stages need their own checks.
Engineers coordinate the drawings and sequence with builders and transit staff so the permanent design can be built.
discussion: Why might a structure that works when complete need extra support during construction?
activity: Sketch a fictional floor across a no-support zone. Trace a load path to the ground and identify a connection that would need checking.
teacher_note: Conceptual force arrows are not an engineered design. Do not suggest students can assess a real building’s safety from a drawing.

roles.collaborators: Architects, technologists, builders and reviewers
roles.classroom_connection: Forces must have a continuous route to supports; an attractive shape alone is not evidence of performance.

question: How can measurements help make a roast repeatable?
hook: Consistency depends on checking what happened, not just repeating a recipe.
company_copy: Phil & Sebastian operates a roasting facility in Calgary’s Simmons Building. The company describes a custom roaster, logged roast data and additional reflectance measurements used to check batches. The story connects food production with instrumentation: recording operating conditions and checking the product answer different questions. Its claims about competitors are not needed for this example.
local_note: The company identifies the Simmons Building as its Calgary roasting facility.
classroom_steps: A roast changes a batch of green coffee through heating. Time and temperature matter, but they do not describe every property of the result.
The company says it records roast data and checks samples with a reflectometer.
A reflectance reading measures how light returns from the sample under specified conditions; it is not a direct measurement of flavour.
Comparing process records with product measurements can reveal variation and guide the next controlled test.
discussion: If two batches have the same recorded temperature history, what else would you want to measure?
activity: Compare three fictional batches: A and B share a heating record but have different colour readings; B and C share colour readings but have different sensory notes. List what each comparison can and cannot show.
teacher_note: The fictional comparisons are not company results. No coffee consumption or hot-equipment activity is required.

roles.title: Roast production
roles.summary: Operate a controlled food-processing sequence and compare the product with its intended result.
tasks: Track batch identity and process settings.
Record observations and measurements during production.

roles.collaborators: Quality staff, technicians and production planners
roles.classroom_connection: Repeating a setting is not the same as verifying a repeatable result.
roles.company_evidence: Company process description supports roasting work; no specific roaster vacancy verified.

roles.summary: Help build and check the equipment that produces measurements. Instrument work joins hardware, software and experiments rather than treating a reading as automatically correct.

roles.collaborators: Scientists, electronics specialists and software developers
roles.classroom_connection: Measurement uncertainty is part of using a tool responsibly.
roles.company_evidence: Custom equipment and reflectance measurements support the work-area connection.

roles.classroom_connection: Repeated results need both measurements and records of the conditions that produced them.

question: How can a moving picture explain a process you cannot see?
hook: A useful animation helps an audience follow relationships that a camera cannot easily show.
company_copy: Broken Pencil Studios is a Calgary creative studio offering animation, illustration and technical visualization. Its own production account describes moving from a communication brief to script, storyboard, design, animation and delivery. The work is not simply making something move: the team chooses what to show so an audience can understand a message.
local_note: The company identifies itself as a Calgary animation production studio.
classroom_steps: Start with the audience and one question the explanation must answer.
Turn the idea into a script and storyboard that show the sequence before polishing the artwork.
Use timing, viewpoint and visual choices to make a relationship visible. A model may simplify reality, so the simplification should be deliberate.
Review whether a viewer understood the intended idea. Revise a confusing scene instead of adding decoration.
discussion: When does simplifying an animation make it misleading?
activity: Draw four frames showing a ball at equal time intervals. Make one version constant-speed and one speeding up. Ask a partner to infer the motion from the spacing.
teacher_note: The ball exercise is our physics extension, not a claimed Broken Pencil client project. Artistic motion may intentionally depart from realistic motion.

question: How can trains share a rail network without getting in each other’s way?
hook: A railway moves through space, but its plan also has to work through time.
company_copy: CPKC operates a rail network across Canada, the United States and Mexico. Its 2025 annual report identifies Calgary as the location of its main operations centre and primary Canadian dispatch facility. Rail traffic controllers coordinate crews and day-to-day locomotive operations. The classroom model below simplifies the scheduling problem; it does not describe railway operating rules.
local_note: Calgary operations centre and dispatch function are documented in the 2025 annual report.
classroom_steps: Two trains can need the same section of track at different times. Distance alone does not reveal a conflict.
A time-distance diagram lets a planner compare movement and waiting in one view.
Changing one train’s departure may affect several later movements. Plans have to consider constraints together.
Real rail operations use formal rules, communication and trained staff. A classroom timetable illustrates only one part of that system.
discussion: What happens to the rest of a timetable when one train is delayed?
activity: On a fictional single-track segment, Train A occupies it from minute 0 to 8 and Train B from minute 5 to 12. Shift B to remove overlap, then discuss what additional safety margin would need a real rule rather than a guess.
teacher_note: This is a scheduling puzzle, not a safe operating procedure. Do not invent braking distances or dispatch clearances.

question: How do you plan water supplies for a city that keeps changing?
hook: A useful water plan asks what might change, not just how much water is available today.
company_copy: WaterSMART, now presented as a Hazen company, works on water management with engineers, environmental scientists and policy specialists. The City of Calgary identifies WaterSMART as a partner in its integrated water-security roadmap and water-reuse assessment. The project supports long-term choices about water supply, demand and reuse; planning evidence does not mean every option has been built.
local_note: Calgary-based work is established through the City’s named roadmap partnership and the company team page.
classroom_steps: Describe the sources and uses of water in the system.
Build more than one scenario for future demand and available supply.
Compare options such as reducing demand or changing which water source serves a use. Reuse requires the right treatment and controls.
Choose actions that can be revised as monitoring and circumstances change. A plan should state uncertainty rather than hide it.
discussion: Would you choose the option that is best in one forecast or useful across several forecasts?
activity: Use fictional annual demand of 100 units. Compare a 10-unit demand reduction under supplies of 120, 100 and 80 units. Identify the remaining deficit and one assumption the arithmetic leaves out.
teacher_note: Units are fictional. Real planning includes seasonality, ecosystems, rights, infrastructure and water quality; subtraction alone is not a water-security assessment.

roles.company_evidence: City roadmap and company team page support water-planning work.

question: Why does a water-treatment system need more than a successful laboratory test?
hook: A treatment idea has to keep working when real water and operating conditions change.
company_copy: Integrated Sustainability is a Calgary-based water-infrastructure business working across design, equipment delivery and operations. Its public project material describes biological treatment of mine water and operating work on a moving bed biofilm reactor. Those are company project claims, not evidence that a mine or treatment plant is located in Calgary. The teaching focus is the connection between a treatment process and the system around it.
local_note: Calgary engineering business; client treatment sites may be elsewhere.
classroom_steps: Identify what is in the incoming water and what quality is required for the intended discharge or reuse.
Select treatment steps that address the target substances. A biological reactor is one possible component, not a universal solution.
Equipment, controls and maintenance must keep the process within suitable conditions.
Measure the outgoing water and compare it with the requirement. A promising test is not the same as sustained operating performance.
discussion: What could change between a successful small trial and a full operating plant?
activity: Compare two fictional plants with equal average output quality: one has stable results and one has large swings. Decide what additional operating records would help explain the difference.
teacher_note: Do not infer compliance from an average or equate all biological treatment processes. No claimed removal percentage is used.

roles.summary: Turn a useful transformation into a workable sequence of equipment and operating steps. Process engineers consider what enters, what leaves and what conditions the system must maintain.
tasks: Draw a flow of materials and energy through the system.

Use trial results to revise the process and communicate constraints.
roles.collaborators: Laboratory staff, operators, mechanical designers and controls specialists
roles.classroom_connection: Conservation of matter and energy connects classroom calculations to process decisions.
roles.company_evidence: Company treatment-design services support process engineering.

roles.title: Water-treatment operations

tasks: Monitor process readings and output tests.

roles.collaborators: Process engineers, laboratories and maintenance teams
roles.classroom_connection: Stable operation matters even when average results look acceptable.
roles.company_evidence: Company project material describes treatment operations; not necessarily a Calgary plant or vacancy.

roles.summary: Keep a process measurable and responsive. Controls work connects sensors, decisions and actuators so the system can respond when conditions change.
tasks: Check whether sensors are reading reliably.

roles.collaborators: Operators, electricians and process engineers
roles.classroom_connection: Feedback uses a measured result to inform the next action.

question: What evidence tells you which contaminated soil needs treatment?
hook: A sample answers a question about a place, a depth and a moment in time.
company_copy: Trace Associates has its headquarters in Calgary and provides environmental science and engineering services. local_note: Calgary headquarters and a Calgary team’s environmental assessment work are documented; the teaching site is fictional.
classroom_steps: Define the question and consider how a substance could reach people, water or other organisms.
Choose sampling locations and depths that can test that explanation.
Compare laboratory results with units, detection limits and the sampling plan visible.
Use the evidence to consider treatment, further investigation or monitoring. One clean sample does not describe the whole site.
discussion: How could a sampling plan miss the part of a site that matters most?
activity: Place six sampling points on a fictional site map containing a former storage area and a drainage ditch. Explain why each point helps test a hypothesis and identify one unsampled uncertainty.
teacher_note: This is a reasoning activity, not an environmental site-assessment protocol. Do not supply a universal safe concentration or ask learners to handle unknown soil.

question: How can a building keep heat in while managing moisture?
hook: The layers around a room have several jobs, and they must work together.
company_copy: RJC provides structural engineering and building-science services in Calgary. Its Calgary building-science leadership describes assessing and rehabilitating building envelopes and roofs. A building envelope separates indoors from outdoors while managing heat, air and water movement. This example uses a generic wall rather than claiming to reproduce an RJC design.
local_note: RJC’s Calgary building-science and restoration team is explicitly identified.
classroom_steps: Indoor and outdoor conditions differ, so heat and moisture can move across a building enclosure.
Materials and joints perform different jobs: insulation, air control, water control and structural support are not interchangeable.
A defect at a joint can matter even when the main wall materials perform well.
Inspection and measurements help identify a cause before a repair is chosen. Appearance alone may not explain the problem.
discussion: Why might adding more insulation fail to fix a water leak?
activity: Annotate a fictional wall section with separate arrows for heat flow, air leakage and rainwater. Identify one joint to inspect and one measurement that would distinguish competing explanations.
teacher_note: The section is conceptual, not construction advice. Correct assemblies depend on climate, materials, codes and professional design.

question: Where does a bakery lose food before it reaches the customer?
hook: Waste can reveal a process problem before a new machine is needed.
company_copy: Calgary Italian Bakery produces bread, buns and other baked goods. A published assessment conducted with Enviro-Stewards and project partners examined food loss and resource use at the bakery. It identified opportunities involving dough transfer, product forming and damage during later handling. These were assessed opportunities, not proof that every proposed improvement was implemented or that the historical figures describe today’s production.
local_note: Calgary bakery; a documented historical facility assessment supplies the specific story.
classroom_steps: Map the steps from ingredients to saleable product.
Measure material losses where they occur instead of combining everything into one waste total.
Investigate a cause: a transfer point, a forming step or later handling may need a different response.
Test a change and compare both waste and acceptable product output. Moving a loss to another step is not a reduction.
discussion: Why is a smaller waste bin not enough evidence that a process improved?
activity: For a fictional 100 kg batch, 6 kg is lost at transfer, 4 kg at shaping and 2 kg at packing. A change cuts transfer loss to 3 kg but adds 2 kg at shaping. Calculate the net change and propose one quality check.
teacher_note: Fictional totals: loss falls from 12 to 11 kg, a 1 kg improvement. This simplified accounting ignores baking moisture loss and is not a real bakery mass balance.

question: How can light and editing make separate shots feel like one scene?
hook: A scene can be assembled from images recorded at different moments.
company_copy: Joe Media Group is a Calgary film and television production company. It describes work in production, editing and colour, and its post-production portfolio includes several formats. The classroom story examines how images are captured and matched. It does not claim that a particular technique or teaching exercise was used on a named production.
local_note: The company identifies a Calgary production operation and Calgary contact location.
classroom_steps: A camera records light from a scene under a particular set of conditions.
Changing the lighting or camera settings can change the appearance of the same subject.
An editor arranges selected shots into a sequence; a colourist can work on differences in their appearance.
Review the sequence for continuity and meaning. A smooth-looking cut is a creative result, not proof that the events happened continuously.
discussion: How can the order of two shots change what a viewer thinks happened?
activity: Draw three shots of the same object with different apparent brightness. Propose a continuity check, then reorder the shots to tell a different story and explain the change.
teacher_note: This is a visual reasoning exercise. Colour grading changes recorded appearance; it does not change the original light source or prove factual continuity.

Keep track of ingredients, processing conditions and batch identity.
Check samples from more than one point in a batch; an average can conceal individual differences.
Investigate a pattern and test one change at a time before deciding whether the process improved.

teacher_note: The figures are invented and no company acceptance limits are implied. Mass comparison does not establish food safety.

question: How can a road cross a creek without ignoring the landscape?
hook: A route has to work for people and for the ground and water beneath it.
company_copy: ISL was the City of Calgary’s prime consultant for planning, detailed design and construction work on the 144 Avenue NW extension. Its project account describes steep terrain, a single-span bridge over West Nose Creek, creek work and multi-use pathways. This creates a local example of design constraints interacting, rather than a story about choosing the shortest line on a map.
local_note: The featured road, creek crossing and pathways are in Calgary; ISL identifies the City as client.
classroom_steps: Map the terrain, existing connections and watercourse before drawing a route.
Compare options for gradients, crossings and access. A change in one constraint can affect another.
Bring transportation, structural, water and environmental expertise together to develop the design.
Check the built corridor against its intended function and monitor the landscape it affects. Design intent is not a measured ecological outcome.
discussion: Why might the shortest route be a poor design?
activity: Choose between two fictional corridors: one is shorter but steep and crosses a creek twice; one is longer and crosses once. List evidence needed before selecting either, without inventing a numerical score.
teacher_note: The exercise is not the actual route evaluation. No claim that the real creek project had a measured biodiversity improvement is made.

question: How can you fit a water-treatment process into a modular unit?
hook: A compact system still needs the right sequence, connections and access for maintenance.
company_copy: ClearBakk is a Calgary engineering company within the ALSYS group. It describes water-treatment and fluid-management work, including modular systems, and ALSYS identifies its design and integration capabilities. The example focuses on fitting a treatment sequence into equipment that can be delivered and operated. A modular package is not automatically suitable for every water source.
local_note: Calgary engineering base; deployment sites and fabrication locations are not assumed to be in Calgary.
classroom_steps: Start with incoming-water characteristics and the required output, not the size of a shipping frame.
Choose compatible treatment stages and account for water, chemicals and residual streams.
Arrange equipment so connections, controls and maintenance access can work within the available space.
Test the integrated system against the requirement. A compact layout is useful only if the treatment and operation also work.
discussion: What could go wrong if a designer only tries to make the equipment smaller?
activity: Arrange four fictional modules on a paper floor plan: feed tank, treatment, output check and residual storage. Draw flows and leave maintenance access. Explain one trade-off when the footprint is reduced.
teacher_note: The layout is invented, not a ClearBakk specification. No water-quality guarantee or operational chemical instructions are supplied.
